title: How to hear this sermon
english: This is a listening version of John Wesley's sermon, Upon Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse Five. It is the sermon as printed in John Wesley's 1771 Works. Rendered in modern English.

title: Not to destroy, but to fulfill
english: Do not think that I have come to destroy the law or the prophets (Matthew 5:17). I have not come to destroy, but to fulfill. Matthew 5:17.

title: One jot or one tittle
english: For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, one jot or one tittle shall in no way pass from the law, until all is fulfilled (Matthew 5:18). Matthew 5:18.

title: The least commandments
english: Whoever therefore breaks one of these least commandments, and teaches people to do so, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:19). But whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. Matthew 5:19.

title: Except your righteousness exceeds
english: For truly I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall in no case enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:20). Matthew 5:20.

title: A teacher of novelties
english: Among the multitude of reproaches which fell on him who was despised and rejected by people (Isaiah 53:3), it could not fail to be one that he was a teacher of novelties, an introducer of a new religion. This might be said with more color, because many of the expressions he had used were not common among the Jews. Either they did not use them at all, or not in the same sense, not in so full and strong a meaning. Add to this that worshipping God in spirit and in truth (John 4:24) must always appear a new religion to those who have so far known nothing but outside worship, nothing but the form of godliness (2 Timothy 3:5).

title: An easier way to heaven
english: And it is not improbable that some might hope it was so, that he was abolishing the old religion and bringing in another, one which they might flatter themselves would be an easier way to heaven. But our Lord refutes in these words both the vain hopes of the one and the groundless slanders of the other.

title: The order of the words
english: I shall consider them in the same order as they stand, taking each verse as a distinct head of the discourse.

title: I have not come to destroy
english: And first, do not think that I have come to destroy the law or the prophets. I have not come to destroy, but to fulfill.

title: The ceremonial law
english: The ritual or ceremonial law, delivered by Moses to the children of Israel, containing all the commands and ordinances which related to the old sacrifices and the service of the temple, our Lord did indeed come to destroy, to dissolve, and utterly to abolish. All the apostles bear witness to this. Not only Barnabas and Paul, who strongly withstood those who taught that Christians ought to keep the law of Moses. Not only Saint Peter, who called the insisting on this, on the observance of the ritual law, a tempting of God, and a putting of a yoke on the neck of the disciples (Acts 15:10) which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear. But all the apostles, elders, and brothers, assembled with one accord, declared that to command them to keep this law was to subvert their souls (Acts 15:24), and that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them (Acts 15:28) to lay no such burden on them. This handwriting of ordinances our Lord did blot out, take away, and nail to his cross (Colossians 2:14).

title: The moral law
english: But the moral law, contained in the ten commandments (Exodus 20:1-17) and enforced by the prophets, he did not take away. It was not the design of his coming to revoke any part of this. This is a law which can never be broken, which stands fast as the faithful witness in heaven (Psalm 89:37). The moral law stands on an entirely different foundation from the ceremonial or ritual law, which was only designed as a temporary restraint on a disobedient and stiff-necked people (Exodus 32:9). This moral law was from the beginning of the world, written not on tablets of stone but on the hearts of all the children of men when they came out of the hands of the Creator. And however the letters once written by the finger of God (Exodus 31:18) are now in great measure defaced by sin, they cannot wholly be blotted out while we have any consciousness of good and evil. Every part of this law must remain in force upon all mankind and in all ages, as not depending on time or place or any other circumstance liable to change, but on the nature of God and the nature of man and their unchangeable relation to each other.

title: To fulfill means to establish
english: I have not come to destroy, but to fulfill. Some have thought our Lord means, I have come to fulfill this by my entire and perfect obedience to it. And it cannot be doubted that he did, in this sense, fulfill every part of it. But this does not appear to be what he intends here, being foreign to the scope of his present discourse. Without question his meaning in this place, consistently with all that goes before and follows after, is this. I have come to establish it in its fullness, in spite of all the glosses of men. I have come to place in a full and clear view whatever was dark or obscure in it. I have come to declare the true and full import of every part of it, to show the length and breadth (Ephesians 3:18), the entire extent of every commandment contained in it, and the height and depth, the inconceivable purity and spirituality of it in all its branches.

title: As old as the creation
english: And this our Lord has abundantly performed in the preceding and following parts of the discourse before us, in which he has not introduced a new religion into the world, but the same which was from the beginning. A religion whose substance is, without question, as old as the creation, being of the same age as man, and having come from God at the very time when man became a living soul. The substance, I say, for some circumstances of it now relate to man as a fallen creature. A religion witnessed both by the law and by the prophets in all succeeding generations. Yet it was never so fully explained, nor so thoroughly understood, until the great Author of it himself stooped to give mankind this authentic comment on all the essential branches of it, at the same time declaring it should never be changed, but remain in force to the end of the world.

title: Until heaven and earth pass
english: For truly I say to you, a solemn preface which denotes both the importance and the certainty of what is spoken, until heaven and earth pass away, one jot or one tittle shall in no way pass from the law until all is fulfilled.

title: Not one iota
english: One jot. It is literally not one iota, not the most insignificant vowel, or one tittle, one corner or point of a consonant. It is a proverbial expression, which means that no one commandment contained in the moral law, nor the least part of one, however insignificant it might seem, should ever be annulled.

title: A word of authority
english: Shall in no way pass from the law. The double negative used here strengthens the sense, so as to admit of no contradiction. And the word, it may be observed, is not merely future, declaring what will be, but has likewise the force of a command, ordering what shall be. It is a word of authority, expressing the sovereign will and power of him who spoke, of him whose word is the law of heaven and earth and stands fast forever and ever.

title: Until all things are fulfilled
english: One jot or one tittle shall in no way pass until heaven and earth pass away, or, as it is expressed immediately after, until all things are fulfilled, until the consummation of all things. Here is therefore no room for that poor evasion with which some have greatly delighted themselves, that no part of the law was to pass away until all the law was fulfilled, but it has been fulfilled by Christ, and therefore now must pass so that the gospel may be established. Not so. The word all does not mean all the law, but all things in the universe. Neither has the term fulfilled any reference to the law, but to all things in heaven and earth.

title: The law and the gospel agree
english: From all this we may learn that there is no opposition at all between the law and the gospel, that there is no need for the law to pass away in order to establish the gospel. Indeed neither of them replaces the other, but they agree perfectly well together. Yes, the very same words, considered in different respects, are parts both of the law and of the gospel. If they are considered as commandments, they are parts of the law. If as promises, of the gospel. Thus, you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart (Deuteronomy 6:5), when considered as a commandment, is a branch of the law. When regarded as a promise, it is an essential part of the gospel, the gospel being nothing other than the commands of the law proposed by way of promises. Accordingly, poverty of spirit, purity of heart (Matthew 5:8), and whatever else is commanded in the holy law of God, are nothing other, when viewed in a gospel light, than so many great and precious promises (2 Peter 1:4).

title: The closest connection
english: There is therefore the closest connection that can be conceived between the law and the gospel. On the one hand, the law continually makes way for the gospel and points us to it. On the other, the gospel continually leads us to a more exact fulfilling of the law. The law, for instance, requires us to love God, to love our neighbor, to be meek, humble, or holy. We feel that we are not sufficient for these things, yes, that with man this is impossible (Matthew 19:26). But we see a promise of God to give us that love and to make us humble, meek, and holy. We lay hold of this gospel, of these glad tidings. It is done to us according to our faith (Matthew 9:29), and the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us (Romans 8:4) through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

title: Every command is a covered promise
english: We may yet further observe that every command in holy Scripture is only a covered promise. For by that solemn declaration, this is the covenant I will make after those days, says the Lord, I will put my laws in your minds and write them in your hearts (Hebrews 8:10), God has engaged to give whatever he commands. Does he command us then to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17)? To rejoice always (1 Thessalonians 5:16)? To be holy as he is holy (1 Peter 1:16)? It is enough. He will work in us this very thing. It shall be to us according to his word.

title: New revelations are of Satan
english: But if these things are so, we cannot be at a loss what to think of those who, in all ages of the church, have undertaken to change or replace some commands of God, as they claimed, by the peculiar direction of his Spirit. Christ has here given us an infallible rule by which to judge all such claims. Christianity, as it includes the whole moral law of God, both by way of command and of promise, if we will hear him, is designed by God to be the last of all his dispensations. There is no other to come after this. This is to endure until the consummation of all things. Consequently all such new revelations are of Satan and not of God, and all claims to another more perfect dispensation fall to the ground of course. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but this word shall not pass away (Matthew 24:35).

title: Break one and teach others
english: Whoever therefore breaks one of these least commandments, and teaches people to do so, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:19). But whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

title: Who reproaches the preaching of the law
english: Who, what are they, that make the preaching of the law a term of reproach? Do they not see on whom the reproach must fall, on whose head it must land at last? Whoever on this ground despises us despises him who sent us (Luke 10:16). For did any man ever preach the law like him, even when he came not to condemn but to save the world (John 3:17), when he came on purpose to bring life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Timothy 1:10)? Can anyone preach the law more expressly, more rigorously, than Christ does in these words? And who is he that shall amend them? Who is he that shall instruct the Son of God how to preach? Who will teach him a better way of delivering the message which he has received from the Father?

title: One point, guilty of all
english: Whoever breaks one of these least commandments, or one of the least of these commandments. These commandments, we may observe, is a term used by our Lord as equivalent to the law, or the law and the prophets, which is the same thing, seeing the prophets added nothing to the law, but only declared, explained, or enforced it, as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.

title: No darling lust
english: Whoever breaks one of these least commandments, especially if it is done willfully or presumptuously. One. For he who keeps the whole law and yet offends in one point is guilty of all (James 2:10). The wrath of God abides on him (John 3:36) as surely as if he had broken every one. So that no allowance is made for one darling lust, no reserve for one idol, no excuse for refraining from all besides and only giving way to one bosom sin. What God demands is an entire obedience. We are to have an eye to all his commandments. Otherwise we lose all the labor we take in keeping some, and our poor souls forever and ever.

title: There is no little sin
english: One of these least, or one of the least of these commandments. Here is another excuse cut off, by which many who cannot deceive God miserably deceive their own souls. This sin, says the sinner, is it not a little one? Will the Lord not spare me in this thing? Surely he will not be extreme to mark this, since I do not offend in the greater matters of the law. Vain hope. Speaking after the manner of men, we may call these great and those little commandments. But in reality they are not so. If we use words properly, there is no such thing as a little sin, every sin being a transgression of the holy and perfect law and an affront to the great Majesty of heaven.

title: Example teaches
english: And shall teach people to do so. In some sense it may be said that whoever openly breaks any commandment teaches others to do the same, for example speaks, and many times louder than precept. In this sense it is plain that every open drunkard is a teacher of drunkenness, and every Sabbath-breaker is constantly teaching his neighbor to profane the day of the Lord. But this is not all. A habitual breaker of the law is seldom content to stop here. He generally teaches other people to do so too, by word as well as example, especially when he hardens his neck and hates to be reproved. Such a sinner soon becomes an advocate for sin. He defends what he is resolved not to forsake. He excuses the sin which he will not leave, and thus directly teaches every sin which he commits.

title: No part in the kingdom
english: He shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven, that is, shall have no part in it. He is a stranger to the kingdom of heaven which is on earth. He has no portion in that inheritance, no share of that righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Nor, by consequence, can he have any part in the glory which shall be revealed.

title: Teachers who break the commandments
english: But if those who even thus break, and teach others to break, one of the least of these commandments shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven, shall have no part in the kingdom of Christ and of God, if even these shall be cast into outer darkness, where there is wailing and gnashing of teeth, then where will they appear whom our Lord chiefly and primarily intends in these words? Those who, bearing the character of teachers sent from God, nevertheless themselves break his commandments, and openly teach others to do so, being corrupt both in life and doctrine.

title: The murderer of his congregation
english: These are of several sorts. Of the first sort are those who live in some willful, habitual sin. Now if an ordinary sinner teaches by his example, how much more a sinful minister. Even if he does not attempt to defend, excuse, or lessen his sin. If he does, he is a murderer indeed, yes, the murderer-general of his congregation. He peoples the regions of death. He is the choicest instrument of the prince of darkness. When he goes from here, Hell from beneath is moved to meet him at his coming (Isaiah 14:9). Nor can he sink into the bottomless pit (Revelation 9:1) without dragging a multitude after him.

title: The easy minister
english: Next to these are the good-natured, good sort of men, who live an easy, harmless life, neither troubling themselves with outward sin nor with inward holiness. Men who are remarkable neither one way nor the other, neither for religion nor irreligion, who are very regular both in public and in private, but do not pretend to be any stricter than their neighbors. A minister of this kind breaks not one, or a few only, of the least commandments of God, but all the great and weighty branches of his law which relate to the power of godliness, and all that require us to pass the time of our stay here in fear, to work out our salvation with fear and trembling, to have our loins always girded and our lights burning (Luke 12:35), to strive, or agonize, to enter at the narrow gate (Luke 13:24). And he teaches people to do so by the whole form of his life and the general tenor of his preaching, which uniformly tends to soothe those in their pleasing dream who imagine themselves Christians and are not, to persuade all who attend his ministry to sleep on and take their rest. No wonder, therefore, if both he and those who follow him wake together in everlasting burnings (Isaiah 33:14).

title: They say he abolished the law
english: But above all these, in the highest rank of the enemies of the gospel of Christ, are those who openly and explicitly judge the law itself and speak evil of the law, who teach people to break, to dissolve, to loose, to untie the obligation of, not one only, whether of the least or of the greatest, but all the commandments at a stroke. Who teach, without any cover, in so many words, What did our Lord do with the law? He abolished it. There is but one duty, which is that of believing. All commands are unfit for our times. From any demand of the law, no one is obliged now to go one step, to give away one penny, to eat or omit one morsel. This is indeed carrying matters with a high hand. This is withstanding our Lord to the face and telling him that he did not understand how to deliver the message on which he was sent. O Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge. Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34).

title: The kiss of Judas
english: The most surprising of all the circumstances that attend this strong delusion is that those who are given up to it really believe that they honor Christ by overthrowing his law, and that they are magnifying his office while they are destroying his doctrine. Yes, they honor him just as Judas did when he said, Hail, Master, and kissed him (Matthew 26:49). And he may as justly say to every one of them, Do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss (Luke 22:48)? It is nothing other than betraying him with a kiss to talk of his blood and take away his crown, to make light of any part of his law under pretense of advancing his gospel. Nor indeed can anyone escape this charge who preaches faith in any such manner as either directly or indirectly tends to set aside any branch of obedience, who preaches Christ so as to annul, or weaken in any way, the least of the commandments of God.

title: Faith that works by love
english: It is impossible indeed to have too high an esteem for the faith of God's elect. And we must all declare, By grace you are saved through faith, not of works, lest anyone should boast (Ephesians 2:8-9). We must cry aloud to every penitent sinner, Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you shall be saved (Acts 16:31). But at the same time we must take care to let all people know we esteem no faith but that which works by love (Galatians 5:6), and that we are not saved by faith unless so far as we are delivered from the power as well as the guilt of sin. And when we say, Believe, and you shall be saved, we do not mean, Believe, and you shall step from sin to heaven, without any holiness coming between, faith supplying the place of holiness. But, believe, and you shall be holy. Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you shall have peace and power together. You shall have power from him in whom you believe to trample sin under your feet, power to love the Lord your God with all your heart and to serve him with all your strength. You shall have power, by patient continuance in well-doing (Romans 2:7), to seek for glory and honor and immortality. You shall both do and teach all the commandments of God, from the least even to the greatest. You shall teach them by your life as well as your words, and so be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

title: The way to destruction
english: Whatever other way we teach to the kingdom of heaven, to glory, honor, and immortality, whether it is called the way of faith or by any other name, it is in truth the way to destruction. It will not bring a person peace at the last. For thus says the Lord, Truly I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall in no case enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:20).

title: Who the scribes were
english: The scribes, mentioned so often in the New Testament as some of the most constant and vehement opposers of our Lord, were not secretaries, or men employed in writing only, as that term might incline us to believe. Neither were they lawyers in our common sense of the word, although the word is so rendered in our translation. Their employment had no likeness at all to that of a lawyer among us. They were conversant with the laws of God and not with the laws of man. These were their study. It was their proper and particular business to read and expound the law and the prophets, particularly in the synagogues. They were the ordinary, stated preachers among the Jews. So that if the sense of the original word was attended to, we might render it the divines. For these were the men who made divinity their profession, and they were generally, as their name literally means, men of letters, men of the greatest account for learning that were then in the Jewish nation.

title: Who the Pharisees were
english: The Pharisees were a very ancient sect, or body of men, among the Jews, originally so called from the Hebrew word which means to separate or divide. Not that they made any formal separation from, or division in, the national church. They were only distinguished from others by greater strictness of life, by more exactness of conduct. For they were zealous for the law in the smallest points, paying tithes of mint, anise, and cumin (Matthew 23:23). And hence they were held in honor by all the people, and generally esteemed the holiest of men.

title: Paul the Pharisee
english: Many of the scribes were of the sect of the Pharisees. Thus Saint Paul himself, who was educated for a scribe, first at the university of Tarsus, and after that in Jerusalem, at the feet of Gamaliel, one of the most learned scribes or doctors of the law then in the nation, declares of himself before the council, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee, and before King Agrippa, After the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee (Acts 26:5). And the whole body of the scribes generally esteemed and acted in concert with the Pharisees. Hence we find our Savior so frequently coupling them together, as coming in many respects under the same consideration. In this place they seem to be mentioned together as the most eminent professors of religion, the former of whom were accounted the wisest, the latter the holiest of men.

title: The Pharisee's account of himself
english: What the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees really was, it is not difficult to determine. Our Lord has preserved an authentic account which one of them gave of himself. And he is clear and full in describing his own righteousness, and cannot be supposed to have omitted any part of it. He went up indeed into the temple to pray, but was so intent on his own virtues that he forgot the design on which he came. For it is remarkable that he does not properly pray at all. He only tells God how wise and good he was. God, I thank you that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this tax collector (Luke 18:11). I fast twice in the week (Luke 18:12). I give tithes of all that I possess (Luke 18:12). His righteousness therefore consisted of three parts. First, he says, I am not as other men are. I am not an extortioner, not unjust, not an adulterer, not even as this tax collector. Second, I fast twice in the week (Luke 18:12). And third, I give tithes of all that I possess (Luke 18:12).

title: I am not as other men are
english: I am not as other men are. This is not a small point. It is not every man who can say this. It is as if he had said, I do not allow myself to be carried away by that great torrent, custom. I live not by custom but by reason, not by the examples of men but by the word of God. I am not an extortioner, not unjust, not an adulterer, however common these sins are even among those who are called the people of God. Extortion in particular, a kind of legal injustice, not punishable by any human law, the making gain of another's ignorance or necessity, having filled every corner of the land. Nor even as this tax collector, not guilty of any open or presumptuous sin, not an outward sinner, but a fair, honest man of blameless life and conduct.

title: I fast twice in the week
english: I fast twice in the week (Luke 18:12). There is more implied in this than we may at first be aware of. All the stricter Pharisees observed the weekly fasts, namely every Monday and Thursday. On the former day they fasted in memory of Moses receiving on that day, as their tradition taught, the two tablets of stone written by the finger of God (Exodus 31:18). On the latter, in memory of his casting them out of his hand when he saw the people dancing around the golden calf. On these days they took no food at all until 3 in the afternoon, the hour at which they began to offer the evening sacrifice in the temple. Until that hour it was their custom to remain in the temple, in some of the corners, rooms, or courts of it, so that they might be ready to assist at all the sacrifices and to join in all the public prayers. The time between they were accustomed to use partly in private addresses to God, partly in searching the Scriptures, in reading the law and the prophets, and in meditating on them. This much is implied in, I fast twice in the week (Luke 18:12), the second branch of the righteousness of a Pharisee.

title: I give tithes of all I possess
english: I give tithes of all that I possess (Luke 18:12). This the Pharisees did with the utmost exactness. They would not leave out the most insignificant thing, no, not mint, anise, and cumin (Matthew 23:23). They would not keep back the least part of what they believed properly belonged to God, but gave a full tenth of their whole substance yearly, and of all their increase, whatever it was.

title: A second tenth to the poor
english: Yes, the stricter Pharisees, as has often been observed by those who know the ancient Jewish writings, not content with giving one tenth of their substance to God in his priests and Levites, gave another tenth to God in the poor, and that continually. They gave the same proportion of all they had in alms as they were accustomed to give in tithes. And this likewise they adjusted with the utmost exactness, so that they might not keep back any part, but might fully render to God the things which were God's (Matthew 22:21), as they accounted this to be. So that, on the whole, they gave away, year by year, an entire fifth of all that they possessed.

title: Not all were hypocrites
english: This was the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, a righteousness which in many respects went far beyond the idea which many have been accustomed to hold about it. But perhaps it will be said it was all false and pretended, for they were all a company of hypocrites. Some of them doubtless were, men who had really no religion at all, no fear of God or desire to please him, who had no concern for the honor that comes from God, but only for the praise of men. And these are the ones whom our Lord so severely condemns, so sharply reproves on many occasions. But we must not suppose that because many Pharisees were hypocrites, therefore all were so. Nor indeed is hypocrisy in any way essential to the character of a Pharisee. This is not the distinguishing mark of their sect. It is rather this, according to our Lord's account: they trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others (Luke 18:9). This is their genuine badge. But the Pharisee of this kind cannot be a hypocrite. He must be, in the common sense, sincere. Otherwise he could not trust in himself that he is righteous. The man who was here commending himself to God unquestionably thought himself righteous. Consequently he was no hypocrite. He was not conscious of any insincerity. He now spoke to God just what he thought, namely that he was abundantly better than other men.

title: Paul was sincere as a Pharisee
english: But the example of Saint Paul, if there were no other, is enough to put this beyond all question. He could not only say, when he was a Christian, In this I exercise myself to have always a conscience void of offense toward God and toward men (Acts 24:16). But even concerning the time when he was a Pharisee, Men and brothers, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day (Acts 23:1). He was therefore sincere when he was a Pharisee as well as when he was a Christian. He was no more a hypocrite when he persecuted the church than when he preached the faith which he once persecuted (Galatians 1:23). Let this then be added to the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, a sincere belief that they are righteous, and in all things doing God service.

title: Do we even come up to them
english: And yet, unless your righteousness, says our Lord, exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall in no case enter the kingdom of heaven. A solemn and weighty declaration, and one which it concerns all who are called by the name of Christ seriously and deeply to consider. But before we ask how our righteousness may exceed theirs, let us examine whether at present we come up to it.

title: Do we dare to be singular
english: First, a Pharisee was not as other men are. In outward things he was singularly good. Are we so? Do we dare to be singular at all? Do we not rather swim with the stream? Do we not many times set religion and reason aside together because we would not look particular? Are we not often more afraid of being out of the fashion than of being out of the way of salvation? Have we courage to stem the tide, to run counter to the world, to obey God rather than man? Otherwise the Pharisee leaves us behind at the very first step. It is well if we overtake him any more.

title: The barefaced extortioner
english: But to come closer. Can we use his first plea with God, which is in substance, I do no harm. I live in no outward sin. I do nothing for which my own heart condemns me. Do you not? Are you sure of that? Do you live in no practice for which your own heart condemns you? If you are not an adulterer, if you are not unchaste, either in word or deed, are you not unjust? The grand measure of justice, as well as of mercy, is, Do to others as you would have them do to you (Matthew 7:12). Do you walk by this rule? Do you never do to anyone what you would not have them do to you? Indeed, are you not grossly unjust? Are you not an extortioner? Do you not make a gain of anyone's ignorance or necessity, neither in buying nor in selling? Suppose you were engaged in trade. Do you demand, do you receive, no more than the real value of what you sell? Do you demand, do you receive, no more from the ignorant than from the knowing, from a little child than from an experienced trader? If you do, why does your heart not condemn you? You are a barefaced extortioner. Do you demand no more than the usual price of goods from anyone who is in pressing want, who must have, and that without delay, the things which only you can supply? If you do, this also is flat extortion. Indeed you do not come up to the righteousness of a Pharisee.

title: The means of grace
english: A Pharisee, second, to express his meaning in our common way, used all the means of grace. As he fasted often and much, twice in every week, so he attended all the sacrifices. He was constant in public and private prayer, and in reading and hearing the Scriptures. Do you go as far as this? Do you fast much and often, twice in the week? I fear not. Once at least, on all Fridays in the year? So our church clearly and absolutely commands all her members to do, to observe all these, as well as the vigils and the 40 days of Lent, as days of fasting or abstinence. Do you fast twice in the year? I am afraid some among us cannot plead even this. Do you neglect no opportunity of attending and partaking of the Christian sacrifice? How many there are who call themselves Christians and yet utterly disregard it, yet do not eat of that bread or drink of that cup (1 Corinthians 11:26) for months, perhaps years, together. Do you every day either hear the Scriptures or read them and meditate on them? Do you join in prayer with the great congregation, daily if you have opportunity, if not whenever you can, particularly on that day which you remember, to keep it holy? Do you strive to make opportunities? Are you glad when they say to you, We will go into the house of the Lord (Psalm 122:1)? Are you zealous and diligent in private prayer? Do you let no day pass without it? Rather, are not some of you so far from spending in it, with the Pharisee, several hours in one day, that you think one hour quite enough, if not too much? Do you spend an hour in a day, or in a week, in praying to your Father who is in secret (Matthew 6:6)? Yes, an hour in a month? Have you spent one hour together in private prayer ever since you were born? Ah, poor Christian. Shall the Pharisee not rise up in the judgment against you and condemn you (Matthew 12:41)? His righteousness is as far above yours as the heaven is above the earth (Isaiah 55:9).

title: A fifth of all he had
english: The Pharisee, third, paid tithes and gave alms of all that he possessed. And in how ample a manner, so that he was, as we phrase it, a man who did much good. Do we come up to him here? Which of us is as abundant as he was in good works? Which of us gives a fifth of all his substance to God, both of the principal and of the increase? Who of us, out of, suppose, 100 pounds a year, gives 20 to God and the poor, out of 50, 10, and so in a larger or a smaller proportion? When shall our righteousness, in using all the means of grace, in attending all the ordinances of God, in avoiding evil and doing good, equal at least the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees?

title: Wherein a Christian exceeds
english: Although if it only equaled theirs, what would that profit? For truly I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall in no case enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:20). But how can it exceed theirs? Wherein does the righteousness of a Christian exceed that of a scribe or Pharisee?

title: Universal, not partial
english: Christian righteousness exceeds theirs, first, in its extent. Most of the Pharisees, though they were rigorously exact in many things, were yet emboldened by the traditions of the elders to set aside others of equal importance. Thus they were extremely punctual in keeping the fourth commandment. They would not even rub an ear of corn on the Sabbath day (Matthew 12:1). But not at all in keeping the third, making little account of light, or even false, swearing. So that their righteousness was partial, whereas the righteousness of a real Christian is universal. He does not observe one, or some parts, of the law of God and neglect the rest, but keeps all his commandments, loves them all, values them above gold or precious stones (Psalm 19:10).

title: The axe at the root
english: It may be, indeed, that some of the scribes and Pharisees tried to keep all the commandments, and consequently were, as to the righteousness of the law, that is, according to the letter of it, blameless. But still the righteousness of a Christian exceeds all this righteousness of a scribe or Pharisee by fulfilling the spirit as well as the letter of the law, by inward as well as outward obedience. In this, in its spirituality, it admits of no comparison. This is the point which our Lord has so largely proved in the whole tenor of this discourse. Their righteousness was external only. Christian righteousness is in the inner person. The Pharisee cleaned the outside of the cup and the plate (Matthew 23:25). The Christian is clean within. The Pharisee labored to present God with a good life. The Christian, with a holy heart. The one shook off the leaves, perhaps the fruits, of sin. The other lays the axe to the root (Matthew 3:10), as not being content with the outward form of godliness (2 Timothy 3:5), however exact it may be, unless the life, the Spirit, the power of God for salvation (Romans 1:16), is felt in the inmost soul.

title: Internal righteousness
english: Thus, to do no harm, to do good, to attend the ordinances of God, the righteousness of a Pharisee, are all external. Whereas, on the contrary, poverty of spirit, mourning, meekness, hunger and thirst after righteousness (Matthew 5:6), the love of our neighbor, and purity of heart (Matthew 5:8), the righteousness of a Christian, are all internal. And even peacemaking, or doing good, and suffering for righteousness' sake (Matthew 5:10), stand entitled to the blessings attached to them only as they imply these inward dispositions, as they spring from them, exercise them, and confirm them. So that whereas the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was external only, it may be said in some sense that the righteousness of a Christian is internal only, all his actions and sufferings being as nothing in themselves, being judged before God only by the tempers from which they spring.

title: Do not fall short of them
english: Whoever therefore you are who bear the holy and venerable name of a Christian, see first that your righteousness does not fall short of the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. Do not be as other men are. Dare to stand alone, to be

title: Singularly good
english: against example, singularly good.

title: Damned for company
english: If you follow a crowd at all, it must be to do evil (Exodus 23:2). Do not let custom or fashion be your guide, but reason and religion. The practice of others is nothing to you. Every person must give an account of himself to God (Romans 14:12). Indeed, if you can save the soul of another, do so. But at least save one, your own. Do not walk in the path of death because it is broad (Matthew 7:13) and many walk in it. Indeed, by this very mark you may know it. Is the way in which you now walk a broad, well-frequented, fashionable way? Then it infallibly leads to destruction. O do not be damned for company. Cease from evil. Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent. At least, do no harm. The one who commits sin is of the devil (1 John 3:8). Do not be found in that number. Touching outward sins, surely the grace of God is even now sufficient for you. In this at least, exercise yourself to have a conscience void of offense toward God and toward man (Acts 24:16).

title: The ordinances
english: Second, do not let your righteousness fall short of theirs with regard to the ordinances of God. If your labor or bodily strength will not allow you to fast twice in the week, still deal faithfully with your own soul, and fast as often as your strength will permit. Omit no public, no private opportunity of pouring out your soul in prayer. Neglect no occasion of eating that bread and drinking that cup which is the communion of the body and blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16). Be diligent in searching the Scriptures. Read as you are able, and meditate in them day and night. Rejoice to take every opportunity of hearing the word of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:19) declared by the ambassadors of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20), the stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1). In using all the means of grace, in a constant and careful attendance on every ordinance of God, live up to, at least until you can go beyond, the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees.

title: The mammon of unrighteousness
english: Third, do not fall short of a Pharisee in doing good. Give alms of all you possess. Is anyone hungry (Matthew 25:35)? Feed him. Is he thirsty? Give him a drink. Naked? Cover him with a garment. If you have this world's goods, do not limit your kindness to a scanty proportion. Be merciful to the utmost of your power. Why not even as this Pharisee? Now make friends for yourself, while there is time, of the mammon of unrighteousness (Luke 16:9), so that when you fail, when this earthly tabernacle is dissolved (2 Corinthians 5:1), they may receive you into everlasting habitations.

title: Offend not in one point
english: But do not rest here. Let your righteousness exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. Do not be content to keep the whole law and offend in one point (James 2:10). Hold fast all his commandments, and utterly abhor all false ways (Psalm 119:128). Do all the things, whatever he has commanded, and that with all your might. You can do all things through Christ who strengthens you (Philippians 4:13), though without him you can do nothing (John 15:5).

title: Little and base and mean and vile
english: Above all, let your righteousness exceed theirs in its purity and spirituality. What is the most exact form of religion to you? The most perfect outside righteousness? Go higher and deeper than all this. Let your religion be the religion of the heart. Be poor in spirit, little and base and mean and vile in your own eyes, amazed and humbled to the dust at the love of God which is in Christ Jesus your Lord. Be serious. Let the whole stream of your thoughts, words, and works be such as flows from the deepest conviction that you stand on the edge of the great gulf (Luke 16:26), you and all the children of men, just ready to drop in, either into everlasting glory or everlasting burnings. Be meek. Let your soul be filled with mildness, gentleness, patience, and long-suffering toward all people, at the same time that all that is in you is thirsty for God, the living God (Psalm 42:2), longing to awake in his likeness (Psalm 17:15) and to be satisfied with it. Be a lover of God and of all mankind. In this spirit do and suffer all things. Thus exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, and you shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
